procedural_history.originating_court: Court of Sessions Judge at Merta in Criminal Original Case No. 1 of 1952.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated the 26th May 1953 of the Court of Sessions Judge at Merta in Criminal Original Case No. 1 of 1952.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants appealed to the High Court of Judicature at Jodhpur. The High Court heard the case as Criminal Appeals Nos. 57 & 83 of 1953 and issued a judgment and order dated the 10th January 1955.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants, having been unsuccessful in the High Court, appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's judgment and order dated the 10th January 1955. The case was heard as Criminal Appeal No. 133 of 1955.

issue.issue_text: Whether a common intention with prior concert can be inferred when a crowd assembles during a chaotic uproar and people rush to the scene.

facts: An uproar occurred in a village at 11 p.m., following reports of thefts.
A crowd of villagers assembled, rushing to the scene of the disturbance.
The villagers armed themselves with whatever weapons they could find.
In the ensuing chaos, some people were beaten, resulting in deaths and injuries.
law: The Court distinguished between "common intention" and "common object."
"Common intention" requires a prior concert, a pre-arranged plan, and a meeting of minds before the criminal act.
"Common object" does not require a prior concert and can develop spontaneously after an assembly has formed.
application: The Court reasoned that in a chaotic situation like a nighttime uproar, it is natural for villagers to rush to the scene with whatever arms they can find.
In such a crowd, individual motives are mixed; some may have an unlawful motive, while many others may have a lawful one, such as apprehending thieves or defending property.
Given the spontaneous nature of the gathering and the varied motives, the Court found it "impossible to say that they were all motivated by a common intention with prior concert."
The Court concluded that one cannot deduce a pre-arranged, shared unlawful plan among all the individuals who rushed to the scene in such circumstances.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that a common intention with prior concert could be inferred. It held that when a crowd assembles spontaneously during a chaotic uproar, it is impossible to conclude that everyone who rushed to the scene shared a pre-arranged unlawful plan, as their individual motives could be varied and lawful.

issue.issue_text: Whether prior consultation is a necessary element for establishing a 'common object' for the purpose of forming an unlawful assembly.

facts: The case involved a scenario where a crowd of villagers, hearing an uproar at night, rushed to a scene where they believed thieves were present.
Some villagers were armed, and the situation escalated into a violent beating of the suspected individuals.
The question arose whether the villagers who participated in the beating had formed an unlawful assembly with a 'common object'.
law: The Court distinguished between "common object" (relevant to unlawful assembly under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code) and "common intention" (under Section 34).
It clarified that "common intention" requires a prior concert and a meeting of minds before the act.
In contrast, a "common object" does not require any prior consultation or pre-planning. The Court explicitly stated, "no prior consultation is required when a common object is in question."
The essence of the distinction between the two legal concepts lies in this requirement of prior concert.
application: The Court explained that an unlawful object can develop spontaneously after people have already assembled for what may have been a lawful purpose.
For example, villagers who lawfully gathered to apprehend thieves could subsequently develop a shared unlawful object to beat them up.
If five or more people come to share this new unlawful object and act together to achieve it, they form an unlawful assembly at that moment.
The object becomes "common" because each person has the same object in view and they act together, not because they planned it beforehand.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition that prior consultation is a necessary element for establishing a 'common object.' It held that a common object can be formed spontaneously on the spot, without any prior meeting of minds, which is the fundamental difference between the 'common object' of an unlawful assembly and the 'common intention' required by other sections of the penal code.

issue.issue_text: Whether an unlawful assembly can be formed spontaneously if five or more persons, who have gathered at a scene, individually develop and share the same unlawful object, even without any prior concert.

facts: A crowd of people gathered at a scene following an uproar, with some individuals being armed.
The initial purpose for gathering may have been lawful, such as apprehending suspected thieves or defending property.
The situation escalated, and some individuals began beating the suspects.
The court had to determine if the people who participated in the beating formed an unlawful assembly, even if they didn't have a pre-arranged plan to do so.
law: The Court distinguished between "common intention" (which requires a prior concert or meeting of minds) and "common object" (which is required for an unlawful assembly).
For an unlawful assembly, a "common object" does not require a prior concert or pre-arranged plan.
An unlawful object can develop spontaneously after an assembly has already gathered for what may have been a lawful purpose.
An assembly is formed when a common factor (like an uproar) induces people to come together. It becomes an unlawful assembly when five or more of its members share the same unlawful object.
application: The Court reasoned that even if people rushed to the scene for a lawful purpose, that purpose could be exceeded.
If individuals began to beat up the suspects instead of lawfully apprehending them, their object became unlawful.
If five or more people developed and shared this same unlawful object (to beat the suspects) and acted together, they would constitute an unlawful assembly at that moment.
The court stated that it doesn't matter if they were instigated or joined in on their own; as long as they acted together with the same unlawful aim, that aim becomes their common object.

The court concluded that there is no difference in principle between an assembly that was unlawful from the start and one that becomes unlawful spontaneously, though the latter is more difficult to prove and requires greater scrutiny.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that an unlawful assembly can be formed spontaneously. It held that if five or more persons, who have gathered at a scene, individually develop the same unlawful object and then act together to achieve it, they form an unlawful assembly, even if there was no prior concert or plan.

issue.issue_text: Whether an appellate court should interfere with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts that an unlawful object developed after an incident began, provided there is evidence to support such a deduction.

facts: A crowd of villagers assembled at night following an uproar, with many arming themselves.
The initial purpose for many was likely lawful, such as apprehending suspected thieves or defending property.

Two lower courts (the 'courts of fact') made a 'concurrent finding' that during the incident, the object of some of the crowd members changed from a lawful one to an unlawful one (beating up the suspects).
These courts found that five or more people shared this new unlawful object and acted together, thereby forming an unlawful assembly.
law: An unlawful object can develop after an assembly has already gathered, even if the initial purpose was lawful.
If five or more persons develop and share the same unlawful object and act together, they constitute an unlawful assembly.
The Supreme Court, when hearing an appeal on special leave, follows a usual practice of not interfering with or re-assessing evidence related to concurrent findings of fact by lower courts.
application: The Supreme Court acknowledged that it was plausible for individuals who lawfully gathered to apprehend thieves to later develop a common intention to beat them up.
The Court explicitly stated, 'It is not for us to re-assess the evidence in special leave.'

It determined that there were circumstances in the evidence from which the lower courts could have logically deduced that an unlawful object developed and was shared by more than five people after the incident began.
Since two lower courts had already examined the evidence and were satisfied that this had happened, the Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with their concurrent decisions.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appeal, holding that an appellate court should not interfere with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts. Since there was evidence from which the lower courts could deduce that an unlawful object developed after the incident began and was shared by five or more people, the Supreme Court declined to review the evidence or set aside their conclusion.

issue.issue_text: Whether the court will entertain a question of prejudice when details are not furnished and the objection was not raised at an early stage.

facts: The appellants argued that they were prejudiced by an absence in the charge against them.
The appellants did not provide any details about this alleged prejudice in their prior petitions.

The appellants failed to raise this objection at an earlier stage, specifically not in their petition to the High Court for leave to appeal, nor in their petition for special leave to the Supreme Court.
law: The court has a general practice of being slow to entertain a question of prejudice when specific details are not provided.
The court will also consider whether the objection was raised at an early stage of the proceedings.
application: The court applied its established practice to the appellants' claim.
It observed that the claim of prejudice was not mentioned at all in the earlier petitions filed in either the High Court or the Supreme Court.
Because the objection was not raised at an early stage and no details of the prejudice were furnished, the court found no reason to entertain the argument.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to allow the issue of prejudice to be raised, rejecting the argument because it was not raised at an early stage and no details were provided.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a common intention with prior concert can be inferred when a crowd assembles during a chaotic uproar and people rush to the scene.
appellant_arguments: It is impossible to deduce a common intention with prior concert when villagers naturally rush to the scene of a chaotic uproar at night, arming themselves for various reasons, including self-defense.
respondent_arguments: The fact that numerous armed villagers assembled suggests there must have been prior consultation and that they arrived in prosecution of a common object.

arguments.issue_text: Whether prior consultation is a necessary element for establishing a 'common object' for the purpose of forming an unlawful assembly.
appellant_arguments: The High Court incorrectly inferred a 'prior consultation', suggesting it was a necessary component for their finding.
respondent_arguments: Prior consultation is not required to establish a common object, as it can be formed spontaneously on the spot. The essence of the distinction between 'common object' and 'common intention' lies in this lack of a requirement for prior concert.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an unlawful assembly can be formed spontaneously if five or more persons, who have gathered at a scene, individually develop and share the same unlawful object, even without any prior concert.
appellant_arguments: The assembly was a spontaneous gathering of individuals in a chaotic situation, not a group sharing a common unlawful object.
respondent_arguments: Even if people rushed to the scene individually, an unlawful assembly could be formed if five or more of them developed the same unlawful object (e.g., to beat up suspected thieves), making it a 'common object' without any prior agreement.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an appellate court should interfere with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts that an unlawful object developed after an incident began, provided there is evidence to support such a deduction.
appellant_arguments: The court should review the evidence because it is unsafe to rely on the testimony of witnesses when other parts of their evidence have been disbelieved by the lower courts.
respondent_arguments: The Supreme Court should not act as a court of appeal on facts and should not review the evidence, especially when there are concurrent findings from two lower courts. Judges of fact have the right to accept parts of a witness's testimony while rejecting others.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the court will entertain a question of prejudice when details are not furnished and the objection was not raised at an early stage.
appellant_arguments: The appellants were prejudiced by an absence or defect in the charge framed against them.
respondent_arguments: The objection of prejudice should not be considered because it was not raised at an early stage (e.g., in the High Court petition or the special leave petition) and no specific details of the alleged prejudice were provided.

cases.principle: The court will be slow to entertain questions of prejudice when details are not furnished, and the fact that an objection is not taken at an early stage will be taken into account.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An unlawful object for an assembly does not require a pre-arranged meeting of minds and can develop spontaneously after people have gathered. If five or more persons, who may have initially assembled for a lawful purpose, subsequently develop and share a new, unlawful object, they constitute an unlawful assembly.
obiter: In a chaotic situation where a crowd gathers, individuals who rush to the scene are presumed to have a lawful purpose, even if armed.
Judges of fact have the right to disbelieve one part of a witness's evidence while acting on the rest of their testimony.
Private persons are no more entitled to beat and ill-treat suspects than are the police.
The court will be slow to entertain a question of prejudice when details are not furnished and the objection is not taken at an early stage.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: An unlawful assembly can be formed spontaneously without any prior consultation. When individuals rush to the scene of a disturbance for what may initially be lawful purposes, such as apprehending thieves, an unlawful assembly is formed if five or more of them subsequently develop and share the same unlawful object—such as beating the suspects instead of apprehending them—and act together in furtherance of that object. This 'common object' is distinct from a 'common intention,' as it does not require a prior meeting of minds. An appellate court will not interfere with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts that such a spontaneous unlawful object was formed, provided there is evidence to support that conclusion.
legal_tests_applied: The essential distinction between a 'common object' and a 'common intention' is that a common object does not require prior consultation, whereas a common intention does.

An unlawful assembly can be formed spontaneously if five or more persons, who may have gathered lawfully, individually develop the same unlawful object and act together, at which point their individual objects become a 'common object'.

An appellate court will not re-assess evidence or interfere with concurrent findings of fact from lower courts in a special leave appeal, so long as there are circumstances from which those courts could deduce their conclusions.
A claim of prejudice will not be entertained if it is not raised at an early stage and if specific details of the alleged prejudice are not furnished.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that the chaotic nature of the assembly made it impossible to find a common purpose, clarifying that a 'common object' for an unlawful assembly can develop spontaneously on the spot without any prior concert.

The court refused to re-assess the evidence, stating its policy of not interfering with concurrent findings of fact by two lower courts which had concluded that an unlawful object had developed after the incident began.
The court dismissed the appellant's claim of prejudice because the objection was not raised at an earlier stage and was not supported by specific details.
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed the respondent's legal position that prior consultation is not required to establish a 'common object,' as it can be formed spontaneously, which is the key difference from 'common intention'.

The court accepted the argument that even if people gathered individually, an unlawful assembly could be formed the moment five or more of them developed and shared the same unlawful object, such as beating the suspected thieves.

The court agreed that it should not act as a court of appeal on facts and should defer to the concurrent findings of the lower courts, as there was evidence on which they could base their conclusion that an unlawful object was formed.
policy_considerations: Private persons are no more entitled to beat and ill-treat thieves than are the police, especially when there is nothing beyond suspicion against them. Exceeding the lawful object of apprehending suspects to unlawfully beat them is a criminal act.
To ensure judicial finality and efficiency, the Supreme Court will be slow to interfere with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts, especially in special leave appeals.
For fairness and procedural order, objections regarding prejudice must be raised at an early stage and with sufficient detail, preventing parties from raising vague, last-minute claims on appeal.
